content: 1. Greenhalgh et al. reported that 5% of wheelchair users found their device difficult to use. In a mixed-methods study, 5% of participants completely disagreed that wheelchairs complicated life, while 3% agreed, and 2% completely agreed that wheelchairs fostered social connection. Among women, 25% completely disagreed that technology caused isolation. 2. Hoenig et al. evaluated wheelchair services provided by rehabilitation experts, which included structured assessments, individually fitted wheelchairs, and additional orders for occupational/physical therapy, equipment, or home modifications as needed. Despite these interventions, there was no significant difference compared to usual care in preventing worsening shoulder pain or improving wheelchair confidence among older, physically disabled individuals. 3. However, the study had a low appraisal score, indicating limited evidence strength. 4. Hansen, Tresse, and Gunnarsson (2004) conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) on wheelchair maintenance. They found that 99% of inspected wheelchairs in the active intervention group required attention, with most defects being simple and easily fixable. Active, structured check-ups reduced accidents and improved safety, but further research is needed to determine optimal check-up intervals. 5. Leochico and Valera (2020) demonstrated the feasibility of telerehabilitation in resource-limited settings. Environmental modifications and real-time video demonstrations were recommended. Patient B had no new deficits and effectively used his wheelchair at home and in the community. Telerehabilitation was positively received, reducing travel fatigue, stress, and costs while improving communication with healthcare providers. 6. Di Marco et al. (2003) emphasized the importance of systematic follow-ups at 3 and 12 months post-wheelchair issuance. These follow-ups allowed users to identify and address problems early, improving the fit between the user and the wheelchair. First-time users particularly benefited from adjustments as their strength, balance, and skills improved. Telephone and face-to-face reviews were effective in assessing user satisfaction, comfort, and wheelchair durability. 7. Best et al. (2005) found that peer-led manual wheelchair training programs improved self-efficacy and wheelchair-related outcomes in community-based users. Training sessions were tailored to individual goals and conducted in various environments, including participants' homes. The program demonstrated significant improvements in wheelchair skills and user confidence. 8. Wheelchair skills training programs for powered wheelchair users, particularly those with stroke, resulted in a 30% improvement in skills compared to no improvement in untrained participants. Training sessions focused on safety, mobility, and advanced wheelchair skills, with significant benefits observed in user confidence and satisfaction. 9. The introduction of long-term wheelchair loan systems and stricter review processes for users requiring multiple wheelchairs led to cost savings and improved service delivery. These changes addressed issues of non-use and functional changes among users. 10. Telerehabilitation using low-cost technology was found to be a viable option in developing countries. Rehabilitation providers should tailor telerehabilitation to the needs and technical capacities of their staff and patients while adhering to ethical principles of telemedicine. 11. Systematic follow-ups and individualized training programs were shown to improve wheelchair fit, user satisfaction, and participation. These interventions highlight the importance of proactive service delivery and the development of clinical guidelines to monitor and enhance wheelchair prescription practices.
